Fabrication and characterization of DPNMs #### 3.3.1. Preparation analysis of DPNMs After the solubility issues in PPP were successfully resolved, this work implemented molecular-level design strategies to advance electrospinning technology through eco-friendly protocols. At 8% (w/v), PVA, a water-soluble and biocompatible polymer, was used as biopolymeric matrix modifier to maximize molecular entanglement in the electrospinning solution. PVA's low toxicity and renewable nature meet sustainable material selection standards for green electrospinning [8]. Importantly, volatile organic compound emissions were reduced by substituting traditional organic solvents like chloroform and DMF [6]. 3.3.2. Fiber structure analysis of DPNMs SEM images and fiber diameter distributions of the electrospun membranes were shown in Fig. 3A. Solution viscosity is a critical parameter controlling fiber morphology: high viscosity (e.g., DPNM-12) resulted in irregular fiber diameters from incomplete jet stretching, whereas low viscosity may cause droplet formation due to insufficient chain entanglement. On the other hand, uniform nanofibers were produced by moderate viscosity (DPNM-6), indicating the best possible balance between chain entanglement and electrostatic drawing. The SEM pictures showed that the NM fiber membrane without L-proLA-PPP had uniformly distributed diameters between 0.04 and 0.055 µm and tightly intertwined fibers that formed a mesh-like structure. Smaller average fiber diameters and a more uniform diameter distribution were the results of segmented liquid flow during spinning, which was made possible by the lower viscosity of the spinning solution without L-proLA-PPP. With fiber sizes mainly ranging from 0.02 to 0.03 µm, the DPNM-6 fiber membrane demonstrated straight, interconnected fibers creating a distinct network topology. It had a better shape and orientation, and it had smaller diameters than the NM fiber membrane. According to these findings, a moderate concentration of L-proLA- PPP may improve the structural integrity of the nanofiber membrane network by increasing the spinning solution's viscosity, decreasing sur- face tension, lowering the average fiber diameter, and achieving a more uniform diameter distribution. Although a fibrous network was also generated by the DPNM-8 fiber membrane, the fibers showed signs of bending, which led to irregular fiber diameters and the development of some thicker individual fibers. On the contrary, the network structure of the DPNM-12 fiber mem- brane showed unfavorable features, such as larger fiber diameters and an uneven distribution, with diameters mostly falling between 0.075 and 0.15 µm. The thicker and less homogeneous fibers were probably caused by the spinning solution's increased viscosity and surface tension, which prevented solution separation under electrostatic forces. The importance of surface tension and viscosity in attaining the ideal fiber distribution and morphology during electrospinning was shown by this analysis [52]. ### 3.3.3. Infrared spectral characterization of DPNMs The DPNM exhibited distinctive absorption peaks similar to those of the individual components, such as PVA, PPP, and the NADES (L-proLA), according to the FT-IR spectrum analysis illustrated in Fig. 3B. The distinctive hydroxyl peaks (approximately 3500–3300 cm⁻¹), C–H peaks (approximately 2900 cm⁻¹), and carbonyl peaks (approximately 1600–1700 cm⁻¹) found in PPP, PVA, and L-proLA are clearly visible in the DPNM, with corresponding shifts that confirmed the composition of the composite and confirming molecular interactions within it. Remarkably, NM's carbonyl peak was located at 1726 cm⁻¹, but DPNMs' was located at 1720 cm⁻¹. The redshift (Δν = –6 cm⁻¹) of the carbonyl peak in DPNMs was attributed to PPP incorporation of the absorption peak shifting to lower wavenumbers. The addition of polysaccharides encourages the material's hydrogen bonds to strengthen [53]. This study demonstrated the critical role of surface tension and vis- costy in determining the shape of fibers during electrospinning. Vari- ations in L-proLA-PPP concentration within PVA-based solutions produced nanofiber membranes with distinct properties. Excessive concentrations resulted in thicker, irregular fibers, whereas moderate concentrations increased viscosity, decreased surface tension, and improved fiber homogeneity. The integration of PVA, PPP, and L-proLA was highlighted by FT-IR analysis, which revealed hydrogen-bond for- mation between PPP hydroxyls and L-proLA carboxyl groups. These results provided important insights for biomedical and cosmetic appli- cations by highlighting the necessity of balancing solution properties for the best nanofiber manufacturing. 3.4. Conclusion This study successfully handled the solubility and transdermal problems of PPP by using NADES technology with electrospinning. L-proLA displayed extraordinary efficacy in dissolving PPP, with a 51.63-fold increase in solubility (4.13 g/100 g vs. 0.08 g/100 g in water) as compared to aqueous systems. Hydrogen-bond interactions between L-proline carboxyl and amino groups and PPP hydroxyl networks impair intramolecular bonds and diminish crystallinity, as indicated by FT-IR spectrum shifts and Kamlet-Taft parameter analysis (a = 2.904). The addition of 30% water improved viscosity and polarity, balancing dissolving efficiency with system stability. The NADES-PPP/PVA system produced nanofibrous membranes with remarkable functionality (diameters ranging from 40 to 150 nm) using electrospinning. Because lactic acid weakens the stratum corneum barrier and the nanofibrous matrix promotes sustained release, DPNM-12, which contains 12 % w/w PPP, achieved 10.11 ± 0.13 mg/cm² cumulative skin permeation over 24 h in pig models. The system's ability to deliver bioactive substances under control was demonstrated by fluorescence imaging, which confirmed dose-dependent penetration and showed that PPP could pass through epidermal layers and accumulate in dermal areas. In addition to >90% fibroblast viability, the membranes demon- strated multifunctional efficacy, exhibiting 95.36 ± 0.17% inhibition of _S. aureus_, 93.59 ± 0.15% suppression of _E. coli_, and 75.8% reduction in inflammatory nitric oxide release. These characteristics, along with the solvent-free manufacturing method and biodegradable ingredients, make DPNMs environmentally friendly options for skincare products that target acne by reducing inflammation and microbial growth. This work promoted sustainable polysaccharide use in cosmetics by fusing nanotechnology and green chemistry concepts. Future work will concentrate on assessing NADES's recyclability, scaling up production procedures, and using _in vivo_ validation to convert laboratory results into clinical efficacy.
